Odin in Godot

1 · What if your scripts were compiled?

3 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
What staysWhat changesWhy botherThe honest costsDo this now

odin_godot lets you attach an .odin script to a Godot node and run it as compiled native code. Scenes, Inspector properties, and engine callbacks remain part of the Godot workflow. The script layout, build step, and debugger change.

What stays#

  • Scenes, nodes, the Inspector, the scene tree. Your game is still built from .tscn files in the editor. Odin scripts attach to nodes exactly like GDScript does: the .odin file is the script resource, with no wrapper stub.
  • @export variables show up in the Inspector with defaults, ranges, enum dropdowns, resource slots.
  • Signals connect in code or the editor.
  • The play button. Save an .odin file and the extension recompiles and hot-reloads it, so the edit → run loop survives.
  • GDScript itself. Odin scripts can coexist with GDScript. You can keep existing UI or editor scripts and migrate gameplay one script at a time.

What changes#

A GDScript class becomes a plain struct and plain procedures:

GDScript
# GDScript
extends Node2D
class_name Mover

@export var speed: float = 120.0

func _ready() -> void:
    print("Mover ready!")

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
    position.x += speed * delta
Odin
//gd:extends Node2D
//gd:class Mover
package my_game_scripts

import gd "godot:godot"

Mover :: struct {
	owner: gd.Node2d,
	speed: f32 `gd:"export,default=120"`,
}

mover_ready :: proc(self: ^Mover) {
	gd.print("Mover ready!")
}

mover_process :: proc(self: ^Mover, delta: f64) {
	pos := gd.node2d_get_position(self.owner)
	pos.x += self.speed * f32(delta)
	gd.node2d_set_position(self.owner, pos)
}

The examples express the same behavior, with three structural differences:

  1. Your state is a struct. Every field is declared, typed, and laid out in memory exactly as written. Tags on fields (gd:"export") replace annotations on variables.
  2. Your behavior is procs. mover_ready and mover_process are free functions taking ^Mover. There is no class, no inheritance, and no implicit self. Post 2 is entirely about what replaces those reflexes.
  3. The node is a field. self.owner is the engine node this script rides on. GDScript blurs your script and its node into one self; Odin keeps them separate, and that distinction ends up mattering a lot.

A code generator (scriptgen, run by the build) reads your file and emits the registration and argument-conversion code in a sibling .gen.odin file. Edit the authored script; the build regenerates that file.

Why bother#

The compile step and fixed data layout affect both execution and framework integration:

Gameplay procedures compile to native code. Arrays and structs have explicit layouts, so loops over gameplay state do not require an interpreter. The Survivors example shows this style of per-frame entity processing; measure your own workload before choosing a language for performance.

State has an explicit layout. Odin provides procedures, structs, slices, and explicit memory management, with no classes or garbage collector. Positions, health, and timers can live together in value types that your code controls.

Kit uses that layout for replication. Kit is the SDK's entity-based multiplayer framework. Its generated field descriptors let a session compare state, build snapshots, and send changes to peers. Tag a field gd:"replicate" to include it in authority-written state:

Odin
Chest :: struct {
	owner:  gd.Node2d,
	net_id: knet.Net_Id,
	x, y:   f32 `gd:"replicate"`,
	gold:   u16 `gd:"replicate"`,
}

The tag declares the field's replication policy. A configured Kit session uses it for networking and snapshots; posts 3–6 show how commands, identity, and session setup add prediction, drop-in joins, reconnects, saves, and migration.

The honest costs#

  • A compile step. Save-to-reload is a compile (a second or two, kept warm), rather than an instant re-parse. Type errors are reported before the new library loads.
  • No in-editor breakpoints. Debugging is prints plus lldb, a real native debugger, but not the one in the editor. Crashes give you symbolized native backtraces naming your Odin proc (Debugging).
  • A new language. Odin uses explicit types, pointers, and memory ownership. Its compiler catches invalid field access and type mismatches, while runtime behavior still needs testing.
  • A toolchain. Everything is pinned in a Nix flake; setup is one page.

Do this now#

Work through Getting Started: toolchain, project wiring, and the Mover above, attached and moving. When it runs, continue to post 2 for composition, cross-script access, and the distinction between the script struct and its node.
